title: The Auditors Institute has noted calls for ATO feedback on how it handles audit contravention reports are common.read more
full_text:
The need for greater feedback from the ATO on audit contravention reports (ACR) lodged by SMSF auditors is a key concern for practitioners and raises questions about the variation in penalties handed out by the regulator, two audit experts have stated.
Auditors Institute director and Assurify managing director David Burrows said he had examined a number of submissions to the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) performance audit of the ATO’s regulation of SMSFs and found many expressed concerns about the lack of information going back to practitioners who flagged issues in an ACR.
“There was a lot of feedback around the process and efficiency of how the ATO goes about reviewing SMSF auditors and the inconsistencies that people experienced,” he stated in a webinar hosted by the institute yesterday.
“There is a sense that an overly prescriptive approach is used and the ATO is looking potentially for perfection in audit files and not understanding the practical considerations auditors face each day.
“For us it is important that feedback be given and for the ATO to acknowledge our professional judgment while auditing.
“The issue that was very consistent in the submissions I looked at was the lack of feedback auditors are getting in relation to ACRs, as well as a concern that administrative breaches, which do not threaten the tax concessions given to SMSFs, were taking the focus away from more serious integrity risks.”
Burrows and Auditors Institute ambassador Graeme Colley also noted there were calls for auditors to have access to redacted ACRs and feedback on their own reports to inform practitioners of what information the regulator was looking for and how it dealt with what was provided.
“The more feedback the ATO provides to auditors, the better information it will get and the more targeted it can get in their compliance work,” Burrows said.
Colley added: “I can see your point because when you look at the guidance from the ATO, it uses a particular language and I doubt they are hiding behind the secrecy provisions by not coming out with practical examples of how they come to the final decision on a particular person.
“However, we have seen cases where the circumstances were basically the same, yet the penalty imposed on one fund over another was quite different and there were no obvious reasons as to why that was the case, and they need to come out with reasons for that.”
author: Jason Spits
